lec05kp22-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp22-losses-27.name: term:Robust loss
lec05kp22-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp22-losses-27.text:
a loss that goes easy on large errors, so a few
bad points no longer dominate the fit.

lec05kp22-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp22-losses-27.name: term:Huber loss
lec05kp22-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp22-losses-27.text:
$|e|\leq c$: $\frac{1}{2}e^2$; $|e|>c$: $c|e|-\frac{c^2}{2}$.
square for small errors, linear for large ones.

lec05kp22-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp22-losses-27.name: term:ε-insensitive loss
lec05kp22-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp22-losses-27.text:
$\max(0,|e|-\epsilon)$: errors up to $\epsilon$ cost
nothing, the excess grows linearly.

lec05kp22-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp22-losses-28.text: For large errors the square shoots up while Huber and ε-insensitive grow linearly: an outlier's influence drops to linear.

lec05kp22-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge

lec05kp22-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp22-hfit-1.name: fig:lec05-kp22-hfit|The same 21 points: the Huber line (c=1) has slope 2.099 and intercept 0.867, close to the clean trend; the least-squares line has slope 2.686, pulled up by the outlier. lec05kp22-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp22-hfit-55.name: term:IRLS
lec05kp22-u01-p3-nf-lec05-kp22-hfit-55.text:
1. start with an ordinary least-squares line.
2. residuals $e$: weight 1 if $|e|\leq c$,
   else $c/|e|$.
3. solve one weighted least squares.
4. back to 2, repeat 100 times.

lec05kp22-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp22-u01-p4-title.text: ε-insensitive regression: only points on or outside the tube are support vectors

lec05kp22-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp22-u01-p4-bridge.text: The Huber slope is off only to 2.10. Another approach ignores small errors: why does that make the solution sparse?

lec05kp22-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp22-tube-1.name: fig:lec05-kp22-tube|A tube of width ε above and below the prediction (here ε=0.2, 60 sine points, RBF SVR). Points inside the tube are within the tolerance and get weight 0; only the 9 points on the tube's edge or outside have weights: they are the support vectors, and those outside reach the cap C. SVR minimises ½‖w‖²+CΣ(ξ+ξ*); ε is the sparsity knob: the wider the tube, the fewer the support vectors.

lec05kp22-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp22-tube-2.name: fig:lec05-kp22-tube#2
lec05kp22-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp22-tube-2.text: The tube and the support vectors (ε = 0.2)

lec05kp22-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp22-tube-424.name: fig:lec05-kp22-tube#424
lec05kp22-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp22-tube-424.text: 9 support vectors, the other 51 points are inside the tube with weight 0

lec05kp22-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp22-tube-426.name: term:SVR
lec05kp22-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp22-tube-426.text:
SVR (support vector regression): minimise $\frac{1}{2}\|w\|^2+C\sum_i(\xi_i+\xi_i^\star)$,
error ≤ tube width + slack
(ξ, ξ* = excess above or below the tube).

lec05kp22-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp22-tube-428.name: term:KKT conditions
lec05kp22-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp22-tube-428.text:
KKT conditions (what an optimum must satisfy), read as:
• error $<\epsilon$ (inside): $\lambda_i=\lambda_i^\star=0$, not a support vector.
• error $\geq\epsilon$ (edge or outside): a support vector.
• error $>\epsilon$ (outside): the weight hits the cap, $\lambda=C$.

lec05kp22-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp22-tube-429.name: fig:lec05-kp22-tube#429
lec05kp22-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp22-tube-429.text: ε is the sparsity knob: wider tube, fewer support vectors

lec05kp22-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp22-tube-431.name: fig:lec05-kp22-tube#431
lec05kp22-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp22-tube-431.text: Ignoring small errors buys sparsity: only the points on the tube's edge or outside carry weights.

lec05kp22-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp22-u01-p5-title.text: The effect of ε: the wider the tube the fewer support vectors (58→2) but the coarser the curve

lec05kp22-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec05kp22-u01-p5-bridge.text: Points on the edge or outside the tube are support vectors and those inside have no weight. How wide should the tube ε be?

lec05kp22-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp22-eps-1.name: fig:lec05-kp22-eps|Sweeping ε (60 sine points, RBF SVR, γ=0.5, C=10; MSE is the mean squared error between the predicted curve and the true sin at 300 equally spaced points): for ε=0.01, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0 the number of support vectors is 58, 29, 9, 6, 5, 2; MSE 0.0008, 0.0020, 0.0038, 0.0175, 0.0551, 0.3455. The larger ε, the fewer support vectors but the coarser the fit; once the tube is wider than the sine's amplitude the curve is nearly flat.

lec05kp22-u01-p5-nf-lec05-kp22-eps-47.text: Larger ε: fewer support vectors (58 → 2), coarser fit: MSE 0.0008 → 0.3455, inside the tube 13% → 100%.

lec05kp22-u01-p6-title.name: u01-p6-title
lec05kp22-u01-p6-title.text: Ridge regression: ε=0 buys a closed form at the price of sparsity

lec05kp22-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp22-u01-p6-bridge.text: The wider the tube the coarser the curve. What do we get if the tube is shrunk to width 0?

lec05kp22-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp22-ridge-1.name: fig:lec05-kp22-ridge|Ridge regression: from SVR set ε=0 and w₀=0; turn the inequality constraints into equalities (the error is exactly the slack ξ_i); the objective becomes minimising C′‖w‖²+Σξ², C′=1/(2C). Closed form g(x)=yᵀ(𝒦+C′I)⁻¹p, with y the target vector and p=(K(x,x₁),…,K(x,x_N))ᵀ, differing from KP21's kernel least squares only by C′I. The price: with ε=0 no point contributes nothing, every point has a weight, and sparsity is lost.

lec05kp22-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp22-ridge-3.name: term:Ridge regression
lec05kp22-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp22-ridge-3.text:
ridge regression: least squares with a norm penalty: besides the squared
prediction error it also penalises the length of the solution.

lec05kp22-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp22-ridge-5.name: term:Closed-form solution
lec05kp22-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp22-ridge-5.text: closed-form solution: the answer comes straight from a formula, no iteration needed.

lec05kp22-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp22-ridge-12.name: fig:lec05-kp22-ridge#12
lec05kp22-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp22-ridge-12.text:
the error is exactly the slack $\xi_i$;
minimise $\mathcal{C}\|w\|^2+\sum_i\xi_i^2$, $\mathcal{C}=\frac{1}{2C}$

lec05kp22-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp22-ridge-17.name: fig:lec05-kp22-ridge#17
lec05kp22-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp22-ridge-17.text: differs from KP21's kernel least squares only by $\mathcal{C}I$

lec05kp22-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp22-ridge-18.name: fig:lec05-kp22-ridge#18
lec05kp22-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp22-ridge-18.text: price: every point has a weight, sparsity is lost

lec05kp22-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp22-ridge-20.name: fig:lec05-kp22-ridge#20
lec05kp22-u01-p6-nf-lec05-kp22-ridge-20.text: ε=0 buys a closed form (no iteration) at the price of sparsity: there is no free lunch.

lec05kp22-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec05kp22-u01-p7-bridge.text: Ridge regression buys a closed form with ε=0 at the price of sparsity. Since it does not resist outliers, what is it good for?

lec05kp22-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp22-collinear.name: fig:lec05-kp22-collinear|The two forms of the linear kernel, w=(XᵀX+C′I)⁻¹Xᵀy=Xᵀ(XXᵀ+C′I)⁻¹y, give w that differ by at most 5.6e-16 (15 points, 4 features, rounding error). term:Collinearity
lec05kp22-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp22-collinear.text:
collinearity: two columns nearly identical, so one
is almost computable from the other.

lec05kp22-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp22-collinear.name: term:Condition number
lec05kp22-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp22-collinear.text:
condition number: ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue;
the larger, the more a small data change makes the solution jump.

lec05kp22-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp22-collinear.name: fig:lec05-kp22-collinear#10
lec05kp22-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp22-collinear.text:
the left solves a system the size of the features, the right

lec05kp22-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp22-collinear.text: A small C′ on the diagonal: condition number 5×10⁸ → 776, coefficients back to (0.49, 0.49); price: shrunk toward 0.

steps.label: Robust regression and ridge regression
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp22 with view-from-text-v2: the pages were planned first and each page is mainly one native infographic, with the terms defined inside the same figure. This unit is self-study: 8 main pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). All experiments (the outlier and Huber fits, the ε sweep, the collinear example, the comparison of four methods, the c sweep) were designed for this lecture and generated by code; rerunning them reproduces the lecture's numbers item by item. The source provides the fact that least squares fears outliers, the three robust losses, the KKT reading and the sparsity of ε-insensitive regression, the closed form and the two forms of ridge regression, and the 'how to remember' summary. English version.

steps.label: The outlier
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP22, following KP21's kernel least squares, which adds up the squared errors of all points. This unit asks what least squares does when one point in the data is wildly wrong. First one term: an outlier is a point far from the trend of the others, an extreme value or a wrong label; it matters more at the edge of the x range. The experiment was designed for this lecture and generated by code: 20 points with x uniform on 0 to 4, random seed 0, y equal to 2x plus 1 plus noise with standard deviation 0.3; then one outlier at (5, 21), 10 above the trend line's 11. The true slope is 2 and the intercept 1. Least squares: on clean data the slope is 2.009 and the intercept 1.000; with the outlier the slope is 2.686 and the intercept minus 0.007. Over three noise draws, seeds 0, 1 and 2, the slope with the outlier is 2.69, 2.95 and 2.98, against 2.009, 2.000 and 1.972 clean. Why: squaring makes an error of 10 cost 100 times an error of 1, so this one point dominates the fit. The next page asks whether another loss can stop one bad point from deciding.

steps.label: Robust losses
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed one outlier dragging the least-squares slope from 2.01 to 2.69. This page asks whether another loss can stop one bad point from deciding. A robust loss goes easy on large errors so that a few bad points no longer dominate the fit. Two common ones: the Huber loss, which for an absolute error up to c uses one half e squared and beyond that c times the absolute error minus half of c squared, square for small errors and linear for large ones, joined at the absolute error equal to c; and the ε-insensitive loss, the maximum of 0 and the absolute error minus epsilon: errors up to epsilon cost nothing and the excess grows linearly. The three curves in the figure: squared, one half e squared, Huber with c equal to 1, and ε-insensitive with epsilon equal to 0.5; they nearly coincide for small errors, with the ε-insensitive loss 0 inside the tube; for large errors the square shoots up while Huber and ε-insensitive coincide and only grow linearly. Numbers: at e equal to 3, square 4.5, Huber 2.5, ε-insensitive 2.5; at e equal to 10, 50, 9.5, 9.5. The next page asks whether the line fitted with the Huber loss is really pulled less.

steps.label: The Huber experiment
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that the Huber loss grows only linearly for large errors, unlike the square. This page asks whether the line fitted with it is really pulled less. The Huber loss has no simple closed form, so IRLS, iteratively reweighted least squares, is used: step 1, start with an ordinary least-squares line; step 2, compute each point's residual e and give weight 1 if its absolute value is at most c and otherwise c over the absolute value of e, so the larger the error the smaller the weight; step 3, solve one weighted least squares with these weights; step 4, go back to step 2 and repeat 100 times; in practice you can stop once it converges. Results on the same 21 points with c equal to 1: the Huber slope is 2.099 and the intercept 0.867; least squares with the outlier gives 2.686 and minus 0.007; clean data gives 2.009 and 1.000. Over three noise draws, seeds 0, 1 and 2: the Huber slope is 2.10, 2.14 and 2.13, least squares 2.69, 2.95 and 2.98. Huber is still slightly off, the truth being 2, but far less, because the outlier's weight is pressed down to c over the absolute value of e. The next page asks why ignoring small errors makes the solution sparse.

steps.label: ε-insensitive regression
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed the Huber slope off only to 2.10. This page asks why ignoring small errors makes the solution sparse. Draw a tube of width epsilon above and below the prediction line. Points inside the tube are within the tolerance and need no weight; only points on the tube's edge or outside have weights, and they are the support vectors. SVR, support vector regression, minimises half the squared norm of w plus C times the sum of the slacks xi and xi star; the constraint is that each point's error is at most the tube width plus a slack; xi and xi star are how far the point is above or below the tube. The KKT conditions are what an optimum must satisfy, read here as: error below epsilon, inside the tube, lambda and lambda star are both 0, not a support vector; error at least epsilon, on the edge or outside, a support vector; error above epsilon, outside, the weight hits the cap C. The figure uses sine data, 60 points, an RBF-kernel SVR with epsilon 0.2: 9 support vectors, the other 51 points are inside the tube with weight 0. So epsilon is the sparsity knob: the wider the tube, the more points inside and the fewer support vectors. The next page asks how wide the tube should be.

steps.label: The effect of ε
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that points on the edge or outside the tube are support vectors and those inside have no weight. This page asks how wide the tube epsilon should be, and what is lost as it gets wider and sparser. The experiment was designed for this lecture and generated by code: 60 points with x uniform on 0 to 2 pi, seed 1, y equal to sin x plus noise with standard deviation 0.15; an RBF-kernel SVR with gamma 0.5 and C equal to 10, sweeping epsilon; the error is the mean squared error between the predicted curve and the true sine at 300 equally spaced points. For epsilon equal to 0.01, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5 and 1.0: the support vector counts are 58, 29, 9, 6, 5 and 2; the MSE against the true sine is 0.0008, 0.0020, 0.0038, 0.0175, 0.0551 and 0.3455; the share of training points inside the tube is 13%, 63%, 90%, 97%, 97% and 100%. The larger epsilon, the fewer support vectors but the coarser the fit; once the tube is wider than the sine's amplitude the curve is nearly flat. The MSE on the right is on a log scale. The next page asks what we get if the tube is shrunk to width 0.

steps.label: Ridge regression
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that the wider the tube the coarser the curve. This page asks what we get if the tube is shrunk to width 0. Ridge regression is least squares with a norm penalty: besides the squared prediction error it also penalises the length of the solution so that coefficients do not get too large; a closed-form solution gives the answer directly from a formula with no iteration. How to get it from SVR: step 1, set epsilon to 0 and w zero to 0, so there is no tube; step 2, turn the inequality constraints into equalities, each point's error being exactly its slack xi, and the objective becomes minimising script C times the squared norm of w plus the sum of xi squared, where script C equals 1 over 2C; step 3, the closed form is g of x equal to y transpose times the inverse of K plus script C times the identity, times p; y is the target vector and p is the vector of K of x and x1 up to K of x and xN. It differs from KP21's kernel least squares only by the term script C times the identity. The price: with epsilon at 0 no point contributes nothing, every point has a weight and sparsity is lost; the loss changes from absolute value to square and the constraint to an equality, so there is no free lunch. The next page asks what ridge regression is good for, since it does not resist outliers.

steps.label: Collinearity and stability
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that ridge regression buys a closed form with epsilon equal to 0 at the price of sparsity. This page asks what it is good for, since it does not resist outliers. The linear kernel has two forms: with a data matrix X with one point per row, w equals the inverse of X transpose X plus script C times the identity, times X transpose y, and also X transpose times the inverse of X X transpose plus script C times the identity, times y. The left solves a system the size of the features, the right one the size of the points; with many features and few points the right is cheaper. The check was designed for this lecture: 15 points and 4 features, seed 2, y also standard normal, script C equal to 0.8: the w from the two forms differ by at most about 5.6 times 10 to the minus 16, which is rounding error. The collinear example: 30 points, seed 3, two columns t and t plus a tiny noise that are almost identical, y equal to t plus 0.1 times noise. Collinearity means two columns nearly identical; the condition number is the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue, and the larger it is the more a small data change makes the solution jump. Ordinary least squares: coefficients (−170.0, 171.0) and a condition number of about 5 times 10 to the 8, which can only cancel by two huge opposite coefficients, so it is unstable. With script C equal to 0.1: coefficients (0.49, 0.49) and a condition number of 776. This is a common numerical stabiliser; the price is that the coefficients are pulled toward 0. The next page asks which of the four methods resists what, on the same data with an outlier.

steps.label: The four methods
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that adding a small positive number steadies the coefficients. This page asks which of the four methods resists what, on the same data with an outlier. On the same 21 points with the outlier, the true slope being 2: least squares 2.686 with 21 non-zero coefficients; Huber with c equal to 1, 2.099, 21; the ε-insensitive linear SVR with epsilon 0.5 and C equal to 10, 2.122, with only 4 support vectors; ridge regression with script C equal to 0.1, 2.679, 21. To remember: Huber turns large errors linear; ε-insensitive ignores small errors and gets sparsity; ridge is epsilon equal to 0 with a closed form and loses sparsity. The common myth is that ridge regression resists outliers. In fact it resists collinearity and overfitting, not outliers: its slope 2.679 is almost the same as least squares' 2.686. This is the last page of the main line. The next page is an extension: how should Huber's threshold c be chosen?

steps.label: Extension: the threshold c
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said Huber resists outliers and ridge does not. This extension page asks how Huber's threshold c should be chosen. On the same 21 points the slope for c equal to 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5 and 20 is 2.045, 2.054, 2.099, 2.188, 2.455 and 2.686. With a large c every error falls in the squared zone, which equals least squares; with a small c the outlier is nearly ignored and the slope is close to the truth, 2. c should be chosen with the noise size, here a standard deviation of 0.3. The next page has two exercises.

steps.label: Extension: exercises
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that the larger the threshold c the more it is like least squares. This page is the exercises. The residual e equals y minus g of x; Huber takes c equal to 1 and the ε-insensitive loss takes epsilon equal to 0.5. Exercise 1: what is the Huber loss at e equal to 0.5 and at e equal to 3? The hint is to decide first whether it falls in the squared or the linear zone. Exercise 2: what is the ε-insensitive loss at e equal to 0.3 and at e equal to 2? The hint is the maximum of 0 and the absolute value of e minus epsilon. Work them out first; the next page is the worked solution.

steps.label: Extension: worked solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page set two exercises. Exercise 1: e equal to 0.5 is at most 1, so one half times 0.25, which is 0.125; e equal to 3 is above 1, so 1 times 3 minus one half, which is 2.5; the square, one half e squared, would give 0.125 and 4.5. Exercise 2: e equal to 0.3 gives the maximum of 0 and 0.3 minus 0.5, which is 0; e equal to 2 gives the maximum of 0 and 2 minus 0.5, which is 1.5. Check: small errors are the same as the square for Huber and become 0 for ε-insensitive; large errors grow linearly for both. This is the last page of KP22; the next KP is the following unit of chapter 4.
